title: Let's Split Up: Zero-Shot Classifier Edits for Fine-Grained Video Understanding
claim: A coarse class label can be edited into several fine-grained subclasses, leaving other predictions unchanged and needing no full retraining.
layout: 2 rows, left-to-right; input videos feed base and edited networks, edit pencil between
description: A left-to-right diagram with two rows. A rounded box on the left holds four stacks of video frames labeled 'Input videos'. In the top row, the frames feed a small neural network, drawn as nodes and edges, with three output nodes in green, blue and yellow. An arrow labeled 'Base Model Prediction' leads to a blue box. That box shows the four videos, each captioned 'Dropping something'. In the bottom row, the same videos feed an edited network. An orange pencil marked 'Edit' points down from the top network. The blue output node now has orange edges fanning out to four new output nodes in teal, gray, light blue and dark blue. An arrow labeled 'Edited Model Prediction' leads to four boxes, each outlined in a matching color. The captions read 'Dropping something into / behind / next to / onto something'. The eye goes first to the contrast between the four identical coarse labels and the four distinct fine labels.
caption: Category splitting aims to edit a trained video classifier by dividing a coarse label into multiple fine-grained subcategories, while keeping all other predictions unchanged. The challenge is to achieve this without retraining the full model and with zero or very few labels.
abstract: Video recognition models are typically trained on fixed taxonomies which are often too coarse, collapsing distinctions in object, manner or outcome under a single label. As tasks and definitions evolve, such models cannot accommodate emerging distinctions and collecting new annotations and retraining to accommodate such changes is costly. To address these challenges, we introduce category splitting, a new task where an existing classifier is edited to refine a coarse category into finer subcategories, while preserving accuracy elsewhere. We propose a zero-shot editing method that leverages the latent compositional structure of video classifiers to expose fine-grained distinctions without additional data. We further show that low-shot fine-tuning, while simple, is highly effective and benefits from our zero-shot initialization. Experiments on our new video benchmarks for category splitting demonstrate that our method substantially outperforms vision-language baselines, improving accuracy on the newly split categories without sacrificing performance on the rest. Project page: https://kaitingliu.github.io/Category-Splitting/.
